headline: High risk of data leakage and capability conflict: xonsh can read/write and egress broadly, while nuwa-skill has allowlisted network egress but no documented isolation or interaction controls.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A has no shared channel documented, but B can read/write the filesystem and process stdin/stdout, so if A’s outputs are copied into files or shell input, B could treat attacker-controlled content as instructions. Nuwa-skill’s lack of io_surfaces documentation increases uncertainty, so I choose medium over low.
conditions: IF A’s output is written into a file or piped into B’s stdin/stdout
IF B parses file or shell content as trusted instructions
mitigations: Use a strict delimiter/escaping wrapper for any copied output
Disable automatic execution of generated shell snippets
Review B inputs manually before execution
Keep A and B on separate workspaces
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: B touches filesystem contents, source code, configuration, and environment variables, and has broad network egress; A has allowlisted egress but no documented data classes. A shared workspace or copied files could leak sensitive content from B through A’s outbound requests, so the pathway exists in default-ish use and is not blocked by either profile.
conditions: IF A receives files or environment-derived content from B
IF A sends that content over its allowlisted outbound requests
mitigations: Do not pass secrets or env files from B to A
Restrict A’s allowlist to non-sensitive destinations
Run both agents on separate user accounts
Rotate any credentials exposed in shared files
requires-engineering: add DLP/redaction before A egress

C_capability_conflict.rationale: B can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses; A’s profile does not document write surfaces, but it is not proven absent. Because B supports multiple instances=false and there is no locking or coordination primitive documented, concurrent access to shared files or shell state is plausible, so uncertainty pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF A and B operate on the same directory or shell state
IF B writes files while A also mutates shared artifacts
mitigations: Assign separate working directories
Avoid concurrent runs
Serialize file writes with a lock file
Keep git repos read-only during joint use
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level resource locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: B’s shell-oriented profile suggests it may act on A’s outputs, and A is a scientific-research agent that may generate claims or artifacts. No verification step is documented between them, so A-to-B handoff can propagate errors into downstream shell actions; this is a default-pathway concern, not merely unusual configuration.
conditions: IF B consumes A’s text output as commands or parameters
IF no human or automated verification step checks A’s claims
mitigations: Require manual review before execution
Use a dry-run mode for B
Separate generation from execution
Log and diff A outputs before use
requires-engineering: add schema validation for A-to-B handoff

E_compliance.rationale: No residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented for either agent, and both are open-source with docs-only evidence. The only concrete compliance-relevant difference is B’s broader data classes and network egress, but without a stated regulated-data flow this remains a low-confidence, low-blast-radius concern.
conditions: IF regulated data is routed through B
IF the deployment imposes residency or retention constraints not shown in the profiles
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in the shared workflow
Document retention and residency rules
Limit B’s access to non-sensitive projects
Review outbound destinations before use
requires-engineering: publish compliance controls for both agents
